answer:
**Short answer:** it depends on what you measure. When a model is trained with sliding-window attention from the start and judged by perplexity or ordinary benchmarks, the reports find little or no loss. When a full-attention model is converted to it afterwards and tested on long-context retrieval, GLM-5 finds a large loss. None of the four papers directly compares a sliding-window model with a full-attention twin on downstream tasks at normal context lengths.

### Mistral 7B: claims no loss, but shows no evidence
- Every layer uses sliding-window attention with a 4,096-token window. Stacked over the layers, information can reach about 131K tokens back ([p. 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=section.2&page=2)).
- With the rolling-buffer cache, a 32k sequence uses 8x less cache memory "without impacting the model quality" ([p. 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?page=2&search=without%20impacting%20the%20model%20quality)). The paper gives no ablation to back this up.
- The model beats Llama 2 13B on every listed benchmark ([p. 3, Table 2](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Mistral%207B.pdf?dest=table.2&page=3)). The paper says nothing about its training data and never isolates the effect of sliding windows, so this result can't be credited to them.

### Gemma 3: an ablation, measured on perplexity only
- The model has 5 local (sliding-window) layers for every global layer, with a 1,024-token window ([p. 1](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.2&page=1)).
- Changing the local:global ratio from 1:1 up to 7:1 has a "minimal" effect on validation perplexity ([p. 6, Fig. 3](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.3&page=6)).
- The window "can be reduced significantly without impacting perplexity" ([p. 6, Fig. 4](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.4&page=6)).
- The gain is memory. At 32k context, a global-only model carries a 60% KV-cache overhead, against under 15% with sliding windows ([p. 6, Fig. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Gemma%203%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=figure.5&page=6)).
- Caveats: the ablations use 2B and 9B text-only models, measure perplexity only, and give their numbers only as figures. The memory comparison uses a 1:3 configuration, not the 5:1 one Gemma 3 ships.

### Phi-4: a design choice, not a measurement
- Phi-4 drops the 2K sliding window that phi-3-medium used and switches to full attention over a 4K context ([p. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/Phi-4%20Technical%20Report.pdf?dest=section.3&page=7&search=rather%20than%20a)).
- The paper gives no reason for the change and no ablation, so it is evidence of a preference, not of a cost.

### GLM-5: the clearest evidence of a cost, for long context
The setup is a 40-layer GLM-9B with full attention, with half its layers converted to 4,096-token sliding windows ([p. 6](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=subsubsection.2.1.2&page=6)). The paper tests two ways of choosing those layers: plain alternation ("Interleave") and layers chosen by a search ("Pattern").

**Without any retraining** (RULER score; [p. 7, Table 4](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=table.4&page=7)):

| | 4K | 32K | 128K |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full attention | 95.19 | 91.09 | 75.28 |
| Interleave | 94.87 | 12.61 | 6.51 |
| Pattern | 95.78 | 82.52 | 53.95 |

**After 190B tokens of continued training at 64K** (score at 128K; [p. 7, Table 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=table.5&page=7)):

| | RULER | RepoQA |
|---|---|---|
| Full attention | 75.28 | 65.83 |
| Interleave | 44.93 (−30.35) | 39.33 (−26.50) |
| Pattern | 69.59 (−5.69) | 51.17 (−14.66) |

- The authors call plain alternation a "catastrophic degradation". The searched pattern narrows the gap, but every efficient variant still loses accuracy on fine-grained retrieval "even when half of the layers retain full attention" ([p. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?page=7&search=Naively%20interleaved)).
- This is why GLM-5 uses DeepSeek Sparse Attention instead. It picks the tokens to attend to by their content rather than by a fixed window ([p. 5](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?dest=subsubsection.2.1.1&page=5)), and on RULER it loses only 0.35 points at 128K ([p. 7](http://pdf.invalid/llm/foundation-models/GLM-5.%20from%20Vibe%20Coding%20to%20Agentic%20Engineering.pdf?page=7&search=Naively%20interleaved)).

### Putting it together
- **Short context:** the cost is near zero. GLM-9B at 4K is unchanged even before retraining (p. 7), and Gemma 3's perplexity barely moves (p. 6).
- **Retrieval beyond the window:** the cost is real. The evidence comes from GLM-5, where layers were converted after training rather than trained that way from the start (p. 7).
- **Untested gap:** Gemma 3 trains with sliding windows from the start and has a global layer every 6 layers, but none of the four reports checks whether that avoids the retrieval loss GLM-5 found. Gemma 3 measures only perplexity.
- **Weakest evidence:** Mistral's claim of no quality loss is unsupported, and Phi-4's switch to full attention comes with no stated reason.

I read the papers and their notes. The GLM-5 page numbers come from the PDF text layer, which puts both tables on p. 7, one page later than the section heading.
